description: I am a resident of Planet Earth (for now!), keeping an eye on humanity's plans to explore the Moon and Mars. But before we send everyone off to space, I thought: why not prepare the next generation of astronauts first? I am a computer science student from Egypt, and as a one-person crew on a mission, I am bringing my programming skills, curiosity and a slightly unreasonable amount of excitement about space to make astronaut training more fun and prepare a few future space explorers along the way
summary: Welcome to Voyage Beyond! For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, I did not just build a game, I built a junior astronaut mission trainer powered by real space data. Kids aged 7–12 take command of their own outpost on the Moon or Mars, where survival depends on every decision. Oxygen runs low, power has to be shared, and when a real solar storm erupts from the Sun, the crew needs shelter before the radiation arrives. But this is not just a story, it is you in action. As the player, you choose your landing site on real Martian terrain, manage your base's resources, and face space weather events pulled live from NASA's own databases. By surviving them, you learn how astronauts plan for life beyond Earth, how NASA monitors the dangers of space, and why every choice on a mission matters.
details:
Kochab's Project Solution 

Voyage Beyond is a pixel-art educational game that teaches children what it really takes to survive beyond Earth, turning real NASA data into an interactive survival mission. Players run a lunar or Martian outpost, balance limited resources, and respond to real space weather events, making space science both fun and accessible.

How Does the Solution Work

  • Players join a crew of astronauts and run an outpost on the Moon (3 sols), then choose a real landing site and survive on Mars (3 sols). 
  • Each sol they get 3 actions to balance oxygen, power, food and radiation shielding. They can’t fix everything, so every choice is a trade-off. 
  • There are 10 mini-games, five for the Moon and five different ones for Mars. In each, the game’s rules and facts come from real NASA data: 
  • Storm Watch / Siren Watch use DONKI coronal mass ejection reports. Players work out arrival times (distance ÷ speed), then shelter the crew. 
  • Tend Garden / Water Loop draw on OSDR space-biology studies and ISS water recycling. 
  • Shield Lab / Regolith Wall draw on RadLab-style radiation research and measured dose rates: about 1.37 mSv/day on the Moon and 0.67 on Mars. Hydrogen-rich materials beat metal. 
  • Landing Site uses Mars Trek map imagery and the real coordinates and elevations of Jezero, Gale, Hellas, Phoenix Plains and Olympus Mons, each with trade-offs between water, safety, shielding and sunlight. 
  • MOXIE Reactor, Refinery, Solar and Rover games are built on Perseverance MOXIE and Mars rover dust records. 
  • The cast is the Warped Portraits characters, and the game includes Canadian Space Agency facts (Canadarm, Radi-N2). Music is an original, generated cinematic space score, so there are no licences to clear. 
  • It runs as a static site that deploys to Vercel. If a live NASA call fails, it falls back to built-in data and says so on screen.

Impact

Voyage Beyond makes NASA data playable by allowing children to interact with real datasets through meaningful decisions and mission outcomes. Through gameplay, players develop transferable STEM understanding, including concepts such as distance, speed, time, resource management, radiation protection, and the trade-offs involved in selecting different planetary destinations. The solution is designed to be accessible and low-cost, requiring only a web browser and working on both desktop and mobile devices without sign-ups, advertisements, or software installation, making it freely available to schools and families. However, some game values are simplified for educational purposes, and I have not yet conducted classroom studies to measure learning outcomes. Looking ahead, I plan to further develop the platform to ensure it is inclusive for all children, including children with disabilities, by incorporating accessibility features and adaptive learning experiences that enable every child to participate in and enjoy space exploration education.

How it meets the challenge

Voyage Beyond is built on real NASA data sources, including DONKI, OSDR, RadLab-based research, and Mars Trek, while clearly labeling any fallback or simulated data to maintain transparency. The experience combines education with engagement through a narrative-driven adventure featuring characters, mini-games, and a scoring system that rewards scientific understanding, such as accurately predicting solar storm arrival times. Designed specifically for children aged 7-12, the game uses simple language, intuitive touch-friendly controls, and short gameplay sessions of approximately 10-15 minutes to suit young learners' attention spans. The solution has been tested end-to-end across all ten mini-games and the complete Moon-to-Mars journey, demonstrating that it functions reliably as a lightweight web application that can be easily accessed through any modern browser. As development continues, I plan to expand both educational content and accessibility features to ensure that children of all abilities, including those with disabilities, can fully participate in and benefit from the experience.

The game benefits 

Children, Parents, Teachers, and the wider community by: 

  • Teaching kids how astronauts survive in space through experience rather than memorization. 
  • Introducing real NASA science, including space weather, planetary maps, and radiation measurements, in a way young players can understand. 
  • Building critical thinking and problem-solving skills through decisions with real consequences. 
  • Bridging the gap between NASA's open datasets and young learners in a fun, engaging way.

My goal 

To make space science more accessible, inspire curiosity, and encourage children to think critically and solve problems, because the next generation of space explorers should not just dream about going beyond Earth, they should start preparing for it. Despite my attempt to reflect real conditions, the game simplifies the science for young learners: time is scaled (one sol is about two weeks), radiation numbers are adjusted for gameplay rather than mission planning, and the offline snapshot uses approximate values. The game also focuses on the Moon and Mars and does not yet cover other destinations or hazards such as micrometeoroids or dust storms.

Tools and Technologies Used 

Coding Languages: 

  • JavaScript (Phaser), HTML, and CSS
  • Browser localStorage → for caching NASA data for 6 hours. 

Design and Media: 

  • Piskel and Warped Portraits by Luis Zuno → for sprites and pixel-style art. 
  • Vercel → for hosting and deploying the game. 
  • Kokoro (open-source text-to-speech) → for the demo video narration.
